items.title: Build Android authentication, session handling and onboarding
items.outcome: As a new user, I can register, verify, sign in, stay signed in safely and sign out from every device, on Android, using the same session rules the server enforces.
items.context: The Android plan has no phase zero: it jumps to debt screens with no authentication, session or onboarding. Everything else on the device depends on an authenticated session, so this is the true first Android ticket.
scope: Registration, verification and sign-in flows matching the server contract
Secure token storage using the platform keystore, never plain preferences
Refresh rotation with reuse detection handled on the client, including forced sign-out
Sign-out on this device and sign-out everywhere
Session expiry, re-authentication prompts and error states
Onboarding shell that sequences consent before any data collection
Discoverable privacy-safe help and support entry from onboarding, authentication and settings
acceptance_criteria: Tokens are stored in the platform keystore and are absent from preferences, logs and device backups
A rotated refresh token cannot be reused; reuse forces sign-out and the user is told why in plain language
Sign-out everywhere invalidates other devices within the published time
Network failure, expired session and revoked session each produce a distinct, recoverable state rather than a crash
Onboarding cannot reach any data collection screen before consent is recorded
All authentication screens are screen-reader traversable and usable at the largest text scale
A user can reach help without signing in, and any diagnostic bundle excludes money, raw messages, provider keys and credentials
contracts_schema: Uses the generated client for the published authentication contract; token shapes are not hand-parsed
security_privacy: Screens carry secure-window protection so credentials do not appear in recents or screenshots
Failed attempts are rate limited client-side and the server limit is respected without leaking which factor failed
observability: Authentication outcome events carry result and reason codes only, never identifiers or credentials
tests: Instrumented sign-in, rotation, reuse and sign-out tests
Keystore storage verification and a backup exclusion check
Accessibility traversal test
Offline and expired-session state tests
Signed-out help navigation and planted-sensitive-value diagnostic scrub tests
rollout_rollback: Ships with onboarding behind a build flag until the consent screens land, then enabled together
Rollback disables new registration but never leaves an authenticated user without a sign-out path
non_goals: Passkey implementation, which follows the authentication decision record
Server authentication logic, which already has tickets
items.parallel_boundary: Primary repo android. Owns the authentication feature module and secure storage. Server behaviour is consumed through the published contract only.

items.title: Build Android manual transaction entry, accounts and category management
items.outcome: As a user, I can add and edit accounts, record a transaction by hand including cash, split it across categories, and manage my own categories, without waiting for automatic capture to work.
items.context: Automatic capture arrives several sprints later and will never cover cash. Without manual entry the application is unusable on day one, and the debt screens have nothing to sit on. This is also the fallback whenever message permission is refused or revoked.
scope: Account creation, editing and archiving for the supported account types
Manual transaction entry with amount, date, account, counterparty and note
Category assignment including split allocation across several categories
User category creation, rename and merge consistent with the category decision record
Editing and reversal of a previously recorded transaction as an explicit adjustment
Offline entry that queues and reconciles through the sync path
acceptance_criteria: An amount is entered and displayed in minor units with no floating point anywhere in the client
A split allocation must sum exactly to the transaction amount before it can be saved, with the remainder rule shown
Editing a recorded transaction produces an explicit adjustment rather than silently rewriting history
Merging a category redirects rather than destroying history and cannot create a cycle
Entry works offline and the queued record appears with a clear pending state
All entry screens are screen-reader traversable and usable at the largest text scale
A rejected server validation is shown as an actionable message, not a generic failure
contracts_schema: Uses the generated client for the accounts, transactions and categories contracts and the published money representation
security_privacy: Amounts and counterparty text are excluded from analytics payloads and from crash reports
Local storage is encrypted and excluded from device backup
observability: Entry funnel events carry step and outcome only, never amounts or counterparty text
tests: Instrumented entry, edit and split tests including the remainder case
Offline entry and reconciliation test
Accessibility traversal test
No-float static check on the client money path
rollout_rollback: Ships with the first Android release; no flag needed because it is the fallback path
Rollback is not applicable; removing manual entry would leave no capture path
non_goals: Automatic capture, which has its own tickets
Budgeting surfaces, which belong to the income epic
items.parallel_boundary: Primary repo android. Owns the entry, accounts and categories feature modules. Server contracts are consumed, never extended locally.

items.title: Build Android statement and file import with a dry-run preview
items.outcome: As a user, I can import a statement file on my phone, map its columns, see exactly what will be created before anything is written, and re-import the same file without creating duplicates.
items.context: Import exists on the server but has no mobile surface, so a user whose bank does not send parseable messages has no way to get history in. Preview before commit is what makes the feature trustworthy for someone importing months of financial history.
scope: File selection and upload from device storage
Column mapping interface with format detection and manual override
Dry-run preview showing creates, updates, duplicates and rejects before commit
Commit step with progress, cancellation and a result summary
Re-import of the same file recognised as idempotent
acceptance_criteria: No record is created until the user commits from the preview
Re-importing the same file creates no duplicates, proven by an instrumented test
A malformed row is reported with its line and reason rather than failing the entire import
A cancelled import leaves no partially committed records
Large files import without blocking the interface and survive process death mid-import
The preview and result screens are screen-reader traversable
contracts_schema: Uses the published import contract with dry-run and commit as distinct operations carrying an idempotency key
security_privacy: The selected file is not copied into a location included in device backup
Import content never appears in analytics or crash reports
observability: Import events record row counts and outcomes only, never content
tests: Instrumented import, preview and cancel tests
Idempotent re-import test
Malformed row handling test
Process death during import test
rollout_rollback: Ships behind a flag for the first release so it can be disabled if a parser problem appears
Rollback disables the entry point; already imported records are unaffected
non_goals: Server-side parsing rules, which the existing import ticket owns
Email and receipt sources, which belong to E28
items.parallel_boundary: Primary repo android. Owns the import feature module. Parsing rules stay on the server.

items.title: Build the transaction timeline with search, detail, edit and reversal
items.outcome: A user can scroll their whole transaction history at a steady frame rate, find a transaction by text, amount or date, open it, correct it by reversal, and understand at a glance whether what they are seeing is pending, offline or stale.
items.context: Every ingestion, ledger and debt ticket produces transactions, and no ticket owns the surface that shows them. The countdown, the debt screens and the simulator all exist, but the list a user actually lives in - the timeline - has no owner, no virtualization requirement and no defined behaviour for the states that matter most: a pending capture, an unsynced edit, a reversal. A list that is not virtualized also becomes the first place the app janks, because a real user's history is thousands of rows.
scope: Virtualized timeline that pages from local storage and holds a steady frame rate over a large history
Search across merchant, note and amount, and filters for date range, account, category and direction
Transaction detail with its ledger entries, its source and its confidence where it was inferred
Edit as a correction, and reversal as the append-only correction path rather than a destructive edit
Pending, offline, stale, empty, loading, error and permission-denied states from the T-UX-01 taxonomy
Grouping and running balance presentation that agrees with the server-derived balance
Deep link into a transaction from a notification or a clarification item
acceptance_criteria: The timeline holds the published frame budget while scrolling a fixture history of at least ten thousand transactions on the minimum supported device
Search returns correct results for merchant text, note text and an exact amount, and states clearly when a filter is active
Editing a posted transaction produces a reversing entry and a new entry rather than mutating the original, proven by a test that reads the ledger after an edit
A pending capture is visually distinct from a posted transaction and never contributes to a balance presented as final
An unsynced local change is shown as such and survives a process death and restart
A stale timeline is labelled stale rather than shown as current, and offline is distinguished from stale exactly as T-UX-01 defines
The running balance shown matches the server-derived balance for the same window, asserted by a test rather than by inspection
Every applicable T-UX-01 state identifier is handled, asserted by the client state coverage check
The screen passes the accessibility and performance budgets applied to the other core journeys
contracts_schema: Consumes the published transaction, category and money contracts through the generated client; money is rendered from the canonical representation and never re-parsed from a formatted string
security_privacy: Raw captured message content is never displayed or stored by this surface; it shows the derived transaction only
Search runs against local storage and sends no query text to the server
observability: Scroll jank, search latency and empty-result rate are recorded so a regression is visible without a bug report
tests: Large-history scroll performance test on the minimum supported device
Search correctness tests across merchant, note and amount
Edit-produces-reversal ledger test
Pending, offline and stale presentation tests
Running-balance agreement test against the server-derived balance
State coverage test against the T-UX-01 identifiers
rollout_rollback: Ships behind a flag with the existing list retained until the new timeline passes its performance budget on a physical device
Rollback re-enables the previous surface; no local schema change is introduced by this ticket
non_goals: Category management and budgeting surfaces, which T-AND-05 owns
Clarification of low-confidence captures, which android#11 owns
Server-side search or export, which the api and compliance tickets own
items.parallel_boundary: Primary repo android. Owns the timeline, its search and filters, the detail screen and the correction journey. The reversal semantics are the server's and are consumed, not re-implemented.

items.title: Implement Android notification permission, channels and token lifecycle
items.outcome: The app requests notification permission at a moment the user understands, registers and refreshes its delivery token reliably, routes every message to a labelled channel the user can control individually, and degrades to local scheduling when permission is denied or revoked.
items.context: Every notification consumer - budget alerts, goal milestones, family and split activity, retention digests, administrative security notices - assumes a delivery path that does not exist. On API 33 and above notification permission is a runtime prompt that a user can deny permanently, and a denied prompt asked at the wrong moment is denied for the life of the install. Channels matter for the same reason: a user who cannot mute the retention digest separately from a security notice will mute everything.
scope: POST_NOTIFICATIONS runtime request on API 33 and above, asked in context rather than at first launch
Notification channels and groups, one per message class, each individually mutable by the user
Delivery token registration, refresh, rotation on reinstall and deregistration on sign-out
Denial and revocation handling, including the case where permission is revoked while a token is still registered server-side
Local scheduling fallback for messages that remain useful without a server push
Deep links from every notification into the surface it refers to, including a cold-start path
Quiet-hours and preference state read from the server so the client and server agree on what may be delivered
In-app cross-channel preference summary with a deep link to the web preference centre and Android channel settings
acceptance_criteria: On API 33 and above the permission is requested in context, and a denial leaves every other part of the app fully usable
Each message class has its own channel, and muting one channel does not mute another, proven by an instrumented test
A token refresh or a reinstall re-registers the device and retires the previous token server-side, proven by a test that asserts the old token is no longer targeted
Signing out deregisters the device so a subsequent push is not delivered to it
Revoking notification permission in system settings results in the server no longer treating the device as deliverable within the published bound, rather than pushing into a void
Every notification deep link opens the correct surface from a cold start, not only when the app is already running
When permission is denied, messages that remain useful are surfaced through the local scheduling fallback or in-app, and the app never re-prompts more often than the published cadence
Quiet hours and per-class preferences set on the server are honoured by the client, and the client never delivers a class the user has disabled
The in-app summary shows server-confirmed cross-channel state and cannot overwrite a sessionless unsubscribe with stale local state
contracts_schema: Consumes the device registration, preference and delivery status shapes published by T-CON-11 through the generated client
security_privacy: Notification payloads carry no financial amount, no merchant name and no other user's identity; the payload is a pointer and the content is fetched after unlock
Sensitive notification content is hidden on the lock screen by channel configuration
Tokens are treated as credentials: never logged, and deregistered on sign-out
observability: Permission grant, denial and revocation rates are recorded per prompt context so a badly timed prompt is visible
Token registration failures and deep-link cold-start failures are recorded separately
tests: API 33 permission request and denial instrumented tests
Per-channel mute isolation test
Token refresh, reinstall and sign-out deregistration tests
Revocation-to-server-stop bound test
Cold-start deep-link test per notification class
Quiet-hours and disabled-class suppression test
Cross-channel preference summary and sessionless-unsubscribe convergence test
rollout_rollback: Enabled per message class, starting with the class with the clearest user value, so a bad prompt context is contained
Rollback disables client registration and the server stops targeting the device; no user data is affected
non_goals: Server-side outbox, scheduling, retries and provider abstraction, which T-NOT-01 owns
The content and cadence of retention messaging, which T-RET-01 owns
Email delivery, which is entirely server-side
items.parallel_boundary: Primary repo android. Owns the permission request, channels, token lifecycle, deep links and the local fallback. The outbox, scheduling and provider selection are T-NOT-01's and are never duplicated here.
